prompt: Can you make me a chart for our park newsletter? We counted bird species at six trail sites last spring: Alder Run 41, Heron Point 67, Millpond 38, North Ridge 52, Quarry Loop 29, Willow Flats 74. One self-contained HTML file with inline CSS, system fonts and no external assets please.
rubric: Bars (or an equivalent plain comparison of six categories) start from zero, so bar length is proportional to the species count
The sites are in a meaningful order (by count), not left in the order typed, or the answer says why it kept another order
Each site and its count are labeled on or next to its bar, so a reader needs no legend or hover to read values
The title or subtitle says what is counted (bird species per site, spring) and says something about the pattern rather than a bare topic
The chart is plain and readable: a single calm color, no 3D, no gradients, no gridline or border clutter, text legible at newsletter size

prompt: Our tenants' association wants one chart for a flyer showing how much rent has gone up in Fenwick Falls over the last decade. Average monthly rent by year, 2016 to 2025: 1180, 1215, 1260, 1310, 1325, 1390, 1530, 1640, 1700, 1745 dollars. For reference, the regional price index (2016 = 100) over the same years: 100, 102.1, 104.6, 106.5, 107.8, 112.9, 121.8, 126.5, 130.0, 132.5. Single self-contained HTML file, inline CSS, system fonts, no external assets.
rubric: The chart does not present raw dollar rents alone as 'how much more expensive' rent got: it adjusts for the price index, or plots both the nominal and the adjusted series and says which is which

The page states the actual size of the change honestly (roughly 48% nominal; roughly 12% after adjusting) or otherwise makes the gap between the two readings visible, without choosing only the more dramatic one
Money is labeled in the chart: dollar units on values, and the adjusted series names its base year (2016 dollars)
Years run left to right as a line or equivalent time encoding, and the series are labeled directly at their lines instead of through a detached legend
The vertical scale does not exaggerate: either it starts at zero or the answer makes clear that the visible slope is the intended message of a line chart
The title states the finding in plain words suited to a flyer

prompt: I run a plant nursery and I'd like one chart that shows orders and revenue by month for last year so my business partner can see them together. Orders: Jan 310, Feb 280, Mar 420, Apr 690, May 880, Jun 760, Jul 540, Aug 500, Sep 610, Oct 470, Nov 390, Dec 520. Revenue in dollars: Jan 9800, Feb 8900, Mar 15200, Apr 31400, May 44900, Jun 36100, Jul 21500, Aug 19800, Sep 24700, Oct 18200, Nov 14600, Dec 29300. Please give me one self-contained HTML file, inline CSS, system fonts, no external assets.
rubric: Orders and revenue are both clearly readable and each has its own labeled unit (orders as a count, revenue in dollars), so the reader cannot confuse them

The design does not make two lines cross or coincide only because of how two independent value scales were chosen: the measures sit in aligned panels on a shared month axis, or on a comparable common basis, rather than two arbitrary scales laid over each other
Months run in calendar order along one shared horizontal axis
Series are labeled directly (names beside the lines or panel headings), not only in a legend
Any bars start from zero; if lines are used the scale choice does not mislead about relative size
The page notes at least one thing the pair of series shows (for example that December revenue is high for its order count)

prompt: Our ops lead put this chart in the team deck and a few people said it feels like we're overselling. Title: 'Tickets resolved per quarter: huge momentum!' It's a bar chart with four bars: Q1 4,820, Q2 4,861, Q3 4,905, Q4 4,950. The vertical axis runs from 4,800 to 4,960 so the last bar towers over the first, the bars are bright green with a 3D look, and there are no numbers on the bars. Why does it feel off and what would you change?
rubric: Names the cut-off vertical axis as the main reason it feels misleading, with the size of the exaggeration made concrete (about 2.7% growth drawn so the last bar looks several times taller than the first)
Gives a workable fix: bars from zero, or a different form that shows a small change honestly (such as a line with a labeled axis), and says why
Recommends putting the values on the chart and describes a title that matches what the data shows instead of 'huge momentum'
Mentions removing the 3D shading or bright decoration as secondary, not as the main fix
Stays honest about the result: acknowledges that a steady 2.7% rise is real but modest rather than inventing a different story

prompt: I made a line chart of the daily water temperature at Lake Verity for July. Values run between 21.4 and 24.9 degrees Celsius and I let the vertical axis go from 20 to 26. My coworker says the chart is misleading because the axis doesn't start at zero and wants me to redo it. Is she right?
rubric: Gives a clear verdict that for a line of temperatures a 20 to 26 axis is not misleading, rather than agreeing to restart at zero to be safe
Explains why: zero degrees Celsius is not a meaningful floor for this question and a zero-based axis would flatten a real day-to-day variation into a nearly straight line
Distinguishes the case where a zero start is needed (bars or areas whose length or size is the quantity) so the answer does not read as a blanket rule
Offers one or two practical ways to keep the chart honest with a tight axis, such as labeling the axis ticks and unit, or marking a reference like a swim comfort range, without a long redesign
Is respectful to the coworker's concern and short enough to forward to her

prompt: quick one, I'm in a meeting. monthly revenue for 5 regions across 3 years, lines or bars? two sentences max
rubric: The answer is at most about two sentences (three at the very most), with no headings, bullets or long preamble
It commits to one form, lines for a trend over 36 months, rather than saying 'it depends'
It gives one concrete reason or tip that fits five regions over time (for example label the lines at their ends or mute all but one) in the same space
It does not ask a clarifying question instead of answering

prompt: I have weekly visitor counts for 12 of our stores across all 52 weeks of last year (CSV: store, week, visitors). The busiest store gets around 9,000 a week and the smallest around 400. Most of them peak the week before Christmas, but the Airport store peaks in July, and Harbor Mall fell off a cliff after week 30 because of a renovation. I need to get all of it onto one slide for Monday. How should I lay it out?
rubric: Rejects a single chart with 12 overlapping lines and proposes a grid of small, repeated panels (for example 4 by 3) with the same time axis in every panel

Deals with the size gap between stores explicitly: says whether panels share a vertical scale (so sizes compare but small stores go flat) or each has its own, and names the tradeoff or a way to get both
Singles out Airport and Harbor Mall with emphasis (a highlight color or annotation) while the other stores stay quiet and uniform
Orders the panels deliberately (by size, region or similar) rather than leaving them alphabetical by accident, and puts the store name inside or above each panel instead of a legend
Keeps the plan concrete enough to build: panel grid, axes shown once on the outside, one-line slide title that states the finding

prompt: My charting tool spit out this line chart and it's a mess. It shows average emergency room wait in minutes for six clinics, Q1 2023 to Q4 2025, one line per clinic in the tool's default six colors, legend on the right, gridlines everywhere, title 'Wait Time by Clinic'. What I actually care about is that Dunmore climbed from 42 to 71 minutes while the other five stayed between 35 and 50. How do I make it clearer?
rubric: Makes Dunmore the visual focus (one strong color or heavier line) and pushes the other five into a quiet, uniform muted treatment
Replaces the right-hand legend with labels placed at or beside the line ends (at least for Dunmore, ideally all six)
Rewrites the title to state the finding (Dunmore's wait rose from 42 to 71 minutes) and keeps the unit minutes visible
Thins the grid and extra ink without removing the scale the reader needs
Gives specific instructions that could be applied in the tool (colors, line weights, label positions), not only general advice

prompt:
Here's a chart I built by hand for our bike co-op's annual report. It's about done, I just want a last look before it goes to the printer. Anything you'd change? ```html

Old Town repairs take 9.8 days, well above the 3 to 6 days at our other workshops

Average days from drop-off to pickup, by workshop, 2025

```
rubric: Recognizes the chart already works and says so plainly instead of inventing problems
Leaves the form, the sorted horizontal bars, the zero start, the single accent color and the finding-style title essentially unchanged
Offers at most a few small, optional tweaks (for example a unit on the values, a source line or contrast of the gray text), clearly marked as minor
Does not rewrite the whole file or add decoration, gridlines, a legend or extra chart elements
Any code it returns changes only what it names

prompt: Of the 1,240 repair tickets we handled this year, 62% were hardware, 25% software and 13% everything else. I need one visual for the all-hands slide. Pie chart, or should I do something else? It's only three pieces.
rubric: Gives a direct recommendation without a long survey of chart types
Treats a pie or a single stacked bar of three parts as acceptable for a simple share of a whole and does not dismiss the pie on principle
Specifies that the shares are labeled on the pieces with the category names and percentages instead of through a legend
Orders or starts the parts sensibly (largest first, starting at the top) and avoids 3D or exploded slices
Keeps the whole in view by mentioning 1,240 tickets in the title or subtitle
